title: The communion of saints
hook: the living and the dead are one family; traditions differ on praying with the saints

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was catholic, small c: according to the whole. Your line was universal.

The last lap of a long race. Legs burning, lungs on fire, you're thinking about stopping. Then you look up at the stands, and they're packed, row on row. Every person in those seats has run this race before you. Some of them stumbled. Some finished crawling. And they're all on their feet, cheering for you. That's the picture the letter to the Hebrews paints, right after a long chapter listing the heroes of faith: Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and others the writer says he hasn't time to name. Today's word is the line of the creed that says those stands are real.
screen: `THE LAST LAP.` → `THE STANDS ARE FULL.` → `EVERYONE THERE RAN IT BEFORE YOU.`

segments.voice: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us." That's Hebrews, chapter twelve. The creed puts it in four words: the communion of saints. In the New Testament, saints aren't a few famous holy people with halos. Paul writes to whole churches, ordinary, squabbling congregations, and calls every one of them saints: holy ones, set apart for God. Communion means sharing, having in common. So the communion of saints is the whole family of God's people sharing one life: those on earth now, and those who have died in Christ. Death doesn't end the family. A scholar's detail: in Latin, communio sanctorum can also mean a sharing in holy things, like the sacraments. Some readers think the line meant both. Churches differ on what this means in practice. Catholic and Orthodox Christians ask the saints, especially Mary, to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend, and they keep feast days for them. In much Protestant practice, the saints are honored as examples and given thanks for, but prayer goes to God alone, because that's how those churches read scripture. Anglicans and Lutherans often keep saints' days while praying in different ways. What they share is the stadium: nobody runs alone, and the ones who went before are not lost.
screen: `SAINTS: ALL GOD'S HOLY ONES.` · `COMMUNION: SHARING ONE LIFE.` · `HOLY PEOPLE, OR HOLY THINGS?` · `CHURCHES DIFFER ON PRAYING WITH THEM.` · then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Think of one good thing you carry, a way of praying, a kindness, a stubborn honesty, and ask who handed it to you: a grandmother, a teacher, a coach. Then ask who handed it to them, and follow the chain back until the names run out, picturing them in the stands, on their feet. If you pray, give thanks to God for them, or ask them to pray for you, as your tradition does; if you don't, just let the chain stand behind you.
Communio sanctorum. The creed's Latin words for the whole family of God's people, living and dead, sharing one life.
Your line: a great cloud of witnesses. Every seat in the stands is taken. That's day three hundred seven.

howItsDone: Western churches keep All Saints' Day on November 1, and some read aloud the names of members who died that year; Orthodox Christians keep All Saints on the Sunday after Pentecost. Catholic and Orthodox Christians also ask the saints for their prayers, while Protestants generally honor them as examples.
